rationale: A wins because it makes the boring, writable story the story: "Figma puts its AI code tool behind a new $25 seat" is a real enterprise-SaaS angle with proof attached. B has energy, but "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" drags the update into a market map the facts never supplied. A shows its caveats; B makes the caveats clean up after the headline has already overpromised.
gaps_in_A: "it lands on 4 million desks" treats total users as guaranteed exposure. The update gives user count, not activation, eligibility, or Make availability.
"What that means for the people who used to draw it" leans toward replacement before the facts prove replacement. The update says prompt-generated layouts, not displaced designers.

"Figma's standalone answer is AI code export" is a little too declarative for the Adobe-collapse angle. A correctly flags the missing collapse date, but that uncertainty should probably demote the angle unless timing is fresh.
gaps_in_B: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overclaims the competitive set. The facts say design-file export plus prompt-generated layouts, not a full prompt-to-app market entry.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is invented market context. Maybe true, maybe not; from this update, it is newsroom contraband.
"Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" is puffed-up strategy narration with no supplied scale, roadmap, or executive framing behind it.
"Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice" assumes paid enterprise adoption from a usage claim. "Used at most Fortune 500 companies" is not the same as "these teams will buy the add-on."
